#6632. With the ‘New’ Yeezy, Ye Says He Wants to ‘Let the Clothes Do the Talking.’ But Who’s Listening?

“I don’t have a lot of words tonight,” Ye told me, not long after concluding his Yeezy Season 01 runway show in Los Angeles on Wednesday evening. “I’ll let the clothes do the talking.”

You might read that quote and be surprised to hear that Ye said it warmly, with an all-32-bared smile. But for those still paying attention, his relatively upbeat demeanor tracks with the tame-not-turnt persona that Ye has performed through most of 2026; the one that’s been slowly-but-surely trying to reamass the cultural capital he’s spent most of the last decade either annihilating or reclaiming. Legions of fans have proven they’re still all in; the culture at large remains justifiably dubious. The question this week is, how will Ye’s return to fashion affect the calculus?

Upon arrival, a typical Hollywood warehouse exterior turned into a Frank Herbert-esque interior as soon as you crossed the threshold. Inside, a hundred or so guests sat on two rows of unbroken benches that encircled a large white mound in the center, lit by a heavenly white glow from above. Inside was a mix of the usual cool kids: models (including the runway-favorite teen rapper Nettspend) and recurring characters in the overarching, enduring Kanye Universe. There was Fear of God founder Jerry Lorenzo, who made conversation with Don C, while 2 Chainz was patiently posted up in a hooded black leather coat like ’98 Wesley Snipes. Big Sean, rebuffing the sweltering indoor temperatures in a shearling jacket over a crewneck sweater, caught up with Hit-Boy.

Models on the Yeezy Season 01 runway, which featured a characteristically minimalist set piece.

The 19-year-old rapper Nettspend walked in the show.

Once everyone was seated, the lights dimmed as the unmistakable opening piano note of “Runaway” set the show into motion, with one lone model striding out in a killer black trench. From there, two more models, men this time, walked out in the opposite direction; what followed was a bit of organized chaos with the number of models and paths alternating at random intervals to the tune of a playlist that zipped between new Ye music (UK garage vibes, it would seem) and a gothic orchestra not unlike the scores Danny Elfman used to chef up for Tim Burton.

The fits were crisp, practical and tactical. Most of the menswear was ready-made for basic maneuvers, while the women’s looks were sleek and casual, with a few Milla Jovovich-in-Fifth-Element skimpy ensembles thrown in because Ye can only restrain himself but so much. The most notable thing, about the guys especially, were the relatively streamlined silhouettes: close-cropped coats, bombers and vests, fitted pants and sweats. Where past Ye lines championed and emblazoned the path for the baggy wave, with oversized boots and pants you could swim in, Ye seemed to be brazenly planting a flag back on the opposite end of the spectrum.

Nearly 12 years, and a dozen lifetimes, since his debut Yeezy Season 1 runway show in 2015, the notion of a “Season 01”—his first formal showing since his damning 2022 show in Paris, the one with the “White Lives Matter” shirts—is a conspicuous attempt to clear the slate. All of his previous shows had been produced in collaboration with Adidas, who severed ties with Ye four years ago, after he tweeted a tirade of antisemetic remarks. This time around, to let the clothes tell it, Ye is locked in. I don’t have an image of every single Yeezy Season line seared into my brain, but I feel comfortable saying Ye’s latest was the first time I looked at one of his collections and objectively thought, I could wear that. Most of the gear is quite solid—and familiar Ye's running the same playbook with Season 01 that he’s run with his music, and to some degree, his persona. It’s the Yeezy gear you know and love(d), refined to make it that much more palatable, similar to the way a song like “Whatever Works” puts him back over chipmunk’d soul samples. And true to the title, it does indeed; the fact that it does is maybe a testament to the brilliance that got lost in the insanity. But is playing the hits (quite literally, with “Runaway” opening the show) what we want from one of the most paradigm-shifting—and absolutely chaotic—creative minds of our time?

Historically, Ye’s designs are so focused on an idea of utilitarianism that they ultimately come off as a bit drab, if not downright dystopian. Essentials like hoodies and beefy leather jackets are still central to his vision, but as the models strode around in his usual earth-toned palette—save for a handful of black looks to start, and a bright pop of reds at the end—it became clear that Ye was putting on the same show in a different kind of stadium. The same sci-fi silhouettes, tweaked to their cleanest shape and most pleasing hue, sans screenprinted hate speech. Ideologically, the runway show wasn’t far off from the experience of hearing his 2007 hit “Good Life” all these years later, ringing off stadium speakers, carrying 80,000 people along on a wave of wistfulness— even if Ye himself only performed approximately 75% of the lyrics against a backing track.

In keeping with all of his other moves this year, Yeezy Season 01 is Ye presenting a safer, rule-abiding version of himself: Ye with just art, no antics. Much in the way that his latest album, Bully, eschewed any lyrics that say, shouted out R. Kelly or Bill Cosby (which is more than can be said about 2024’s Vultures 1), it felt like a deep sigh of relief to see him present clothes that don’t feature appalling slogans, at a fashion show with Candace Owens nowhere in sight. But the compromise for a sanitized Kanye is also one that can’t help but feel anodyne as well. The New Ye doesn’t needle, but he’s lost Old Ye’s knack for trying something new. Of course, we’re also well over a decade into the Yeezy experiment—at this point, the present has caught up to the futuristic vision Ye first dreamt up back in 2015. There’s a whole new generation of aspiring designers creating in his image, kids who fancy themselves trailblazers whose paths just loop back to Ye: streamer Kai Cenat just launched his own clothing brand, Vivet, while N3on attended Wednesday night’s show, skipping the Yeezy space gleefully documenting every interaction. It feels as though all of this has happened before, and all of it will happen again.

Mystery. Intrigue. Chaos. This is the typical life cycle for a Ye project, be it music, fashion, or otherwise. An announcement materializes, hype ensues. Then, inevitably, the seams start to show and it becomes apparent that he isn’t inviting you on a pre-planned journey so much as building the plane in real time, seconds before takeoff. And then, through sheer force of will, or maybe even genius, the result ends up so captivating that the speedbumps hardly matter. He’s still a master showman, and all it takes is a strong yearning for the Old Ye to find yourself surrendering to it. The efficacy of that last factor, though, has undeniably waned over the years. For much of the 2020s, in the midst of many a manic outburst or worse, Ye’s messes have hardly cohered into something objectively beautiful. The intrigue curdled into perverse bemusement; for every unwavering diehard fan, there was a rubbernecker tapped in to watch the circus.

The 2026 version of Ye has been an exercise in proving how many people will show up when he shuts up, and whether he can make it back from the brink if he delivers the right spectacle.

The result is the most well-oiled the Yeezy Machine has ever been. An album that more or less dropped when he said it would, for once. A smattering of live shows across the world, each in a sold-out stadium boasting record-breaking rap concert attendance where he leans on his most enduring strengths: visual spectacle and a bulletproof catalog. The only area left to renegotiate is fashion…which brings us back to Wednesday night in LA.

These are the scenes you’d expect at a Ye event, but the first sign that the overall vibe was different and more relaxed was that the man himself was at the door, tucked off into a hallway, immaculately dressed in a fitted all-black leather fit offset by a ridiculously large and ornate gold waist fixture—every bit the Dune-caliber fit as the space we were standing in required. Ahead of the show, he posed backstage flanked by his wife, Bianca Censori, and the four kids he shares with his ex, Kim Kardashian (including 13-year-old North, who was sporting her unmistakable blue-raspberry locks). At Yeezy events past, you’d expect to see harried staff scrambling, while Ye was somewhere out of sight but exuding stress and anxiety out into the atmosphere. But on Wednesday, the 49-year-old beamed as friends made their way past him to their seats. Even a three-piece-suited Kid Cudi came over to say hello.

Ye backstage with his children, from left: North, Psalm, Chicago, and Saint West.

Fifteen years ago, Yeezy Season 01 would’ve caused a massive sea change in the menswear world almost instantaneously, with the wave starting in SoHo then slowly emanating out into the beyond. In 2026, does Kanye still move that needle? The Year in Ye has been one big display of his ability to Don Draper the culture at large, and shock us all by “how much it never happened.” There’s no controversy big enough to keep him away for too long and very few fences he can’t mend.

For example, Sean and Cudi ceased their umpteenth falling out with their old label boss two months ago at a guest-packed, blockbuster homecoming show in Chicago on Ye’s tour stop; their show of support tonight only underlined how deeply the hatchet has been buried yet again. When I spoke to Big Sean after the show, he could only marvel at how much Ye has “given” to the culture across all different categories. One-time GOOD Music COO Steven Victor said the show made him feel like Ye “has his shit together,” noting that Ye admitted to him that he was still working out the model patterns hours before showtime. In past Yeezy Seasons, the cram-effect would’ve been apparent, but here, Victor said he wouldn’t have noticed because it all seemed to go off so effortlessly.

As for the man himself? I spoke to him, but again, he didn’t have much to say, at least on the record. He seemed excited that I picked up on the intentional disharmony of the model routes, and explained that the space we were standing in was a “language I’ve been working on for 10 years” called “DROAM,” which refers to the minimalist design he hopes to apply to stores, urban planning, and a home for himself.

“I got a quote for you,” Victor interjected. “The king returns!” Ye laughed. The question remains, though: Is he welcome?

#6631. Slow-Cooker Tuscan Chicken

Creamy Tuscan chicken is a Delish classic—it’s by far one of our most-made meals. This slow-cooker variation is perfect for a busy fall night and has all of the flavors of the original—garlic, cherry tomatoes, oregano, and Parm—plus the added benefit of hands-off cooking. The other thing I love about this recipe (perhaps more than the original, but don't tell!) is that it uses bone-in chicken thighs, which are my favorite cut of chicken. Chicken breast is great for the OG stovetop version, but thighs are far more forgiving for low and slow heat, and they offer a little bit of extra flavor from the bone and skin.

The potatoes:When you have a creamy, delicious slow-cooker meal hot and ready to eat, the last thing you want to do is take out an extra pot to make a side dish, so we broke the Tuscan formula ever so slightly by adding baby potatoes to make this a well-rounded and hearty main and side all in one. It’s my new go-to on busy weeknights, and it provides all the comfort of the original, with even more oomph.

Storage:If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

#6630. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6629. The Deeper Meaning Behind Kate Middleton’s Remembrance Day Earrings

Kate Middleton’s jewelry choices often carry a significance beyond their sparkle. Across this year’s Remembrance commemorations, the Princess of Wales paid subtle tributes to two of the most significant women in the royal family’s history: Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana. And the personal stories behind her chosen earrings offered a poignant reminder of how royal jewels are passed between generations.

On Sunday morning, Kate joined senior members of the royal family for the National Service of Remembrance at London’s Cenotaph, where King Charles III and Prince William laid wreaths in honor of those who have lost their lives in military service. Watching from a balcony alongside Queen Camilla, the Princess wore a sharply tailored black Catherine Walker coat (a new addition to her wardrobe, from a long-favored designer that Diana also loved), with a double-breasted silhouette, velvet buttons, and a high velvet collar, topped with an asymmetric wide-brimmed hat by Jane Taylor. But it was the familiar pearl-and-diamond earrings that carried a particularly personal significance.

The Collingwood Pearl and Diamond Drop Earrings once belonged to her late mother-in-law, Princess Diana. Given to Diana by London jewelers Collingwood ahead of her wedding to the then-Prince Charles in 1981, the earrings feature diamond-studded settings from which large, lustrous pearls are suspended. They became a mainstay of Diana's jewelry collection, accompanying her to glittering state banquets and royal engagements. In the years since, Kate has made the heirlooms part of her own wardrobe, continuing their story as the current Princess of Wales and wearing them on multiple royal engagements.

There was further symbolism in Sunday’s accessories. Kate fastened three red poppies to her coat alongside the HMS Glasgow Brooch, a sterling silver piece specially commissioned by Glasgow jeweler James Porter & Son in 2025 to mark her role as sponsor of the Royal Navy warship. Its design incorporates the ship’s crest, the Scottish thistle, and a depiction of St. Kentigern, Glasgow's patron saint. The three poppies, have been linked to Kate’s own family history: three brothers of her great-grandmother Olive were killed during the First World War, although the Princess has never publicly confirmed the connection.

The previous evening, Kate had reached for a different pair of royal heirlooms. Attending the Royal British Legion’s Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall with Prince William, she wore Queen Elizabeth II’s Diamond Orbital Pendant Earrings, also known as the Queen’s Diamond Frame Earrings. The intricate jewels feature a floral diamond cluster at the ear and a cascade of graduating diamonds enclosed within a glittering frame. While their precise origins remain unknown, Elizabeth wore them on several occasions, including the State Opening of Parliament in 2012.

Kate Middleton first wore the earrings publicly in 2016 and has since chosen them for significant moments, including Princess Eugenie’s wedding in 2018 and her own official 40th birthday portraits in 2022. For Saturday’s ceremony, she paired them with a black-and-white pleated polka-dot dress by Alessandra Rich—another sentimental wardrobe repeat, having previously worn it to Prince Philip’s memorial service at Westminster Abbey in March 2022. A black suede Ba&Sh belt, pointed Alessandra Rich slingbacks, a velvet Jimmy Choo clutch, and her Irish Guards Regimental Brooch finished the ensemble.

Across two consecutive days, the Princess’s choices traced a line through three generations of royal women. From Elizabeth’s glittering diamonds to Diana’s unmistakable pearls, these were jewels carrying memories as well as history. And at a time of national reflection, Kate’s wardrobe offered its own quiet tribute to those who came before her.

#6626. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.

Olivia Maule is a former Live Science intern and science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

#6624. A Visit With Six Women Farmers Across the Americas

Women make up nearly half of the agricultural workforce in developing countries, yet they account for fewer than one in five of the world’s agricultural landholders. As rising food prices, climate volatility, and food security concerns put farming back at the center of public debate, the United Nations designated 2026 as the International Year of the Woman Farmer, bringing renewed attention to a workforce that remains central to food systems while often excluded from land ownership, financing, and decision-making.

Between January and August 2026, I spent two weeks living with each of six women farmers. In the Galápagos, María Espinoza grows food without chemicals on islands that still import most of what they eat. In Guatemala, Aurelia Beb Tec cultivates cacao on land returned to her Q’eqchi’ community through a reparations process after decades of dispossession and war. In Chiapas, Yumara Salas Ramírez became the first woman to serve as secretary of her coffee cooperative. In Haiti, Lucianie Vil, a 70-year-old Madan Sara, carries her harvest by mule to the border market of Anse-à-Pitre. In Arkansas, Samantha Noble coordinates poultry production at a ranch devoted to regenerative farming. And in Honduras, Milexy Rodríguez lost 15 cows in 40 days when drought dried up her lagoon, rebuilding by drilling a well and diversifying.

The resulting photographs follow the rhythm of their days and the pressures shaping food production where they live. They also show what these women have built: cooperatives, savings groups, a coffee brand of their own, knowledge passed on to their daughters and neighbors.

María Espinoza, 54, lives in the highlands of San Cristóbal Island, in the Galápagos. She is up at 5 a.m. to feed her animals before heading into the fields, where she grows fruit and vegetables on a plot she slowly reclaimed from invasive blackberry. She lives alone but the farm sets the rhythm of her day, keeps her company, and puts food on the table.

Fresh water on the island is scarce and depends on El Junco lagoon, while pests and food shipped in from the mainland make farming hard. María uses no chemicals, makes her own organic fertilizers, and, since 2023, has trained in protecting soil and crops without pesticides.

María Espinoza gets dressed in her bedroom before heading out to work on her farm.

Espinoza pushes a wheelbarrow loaded with freshly harvested produce. Back home, she will wash and prepare it to take to market the next day.

Espinoza tends her stall at the agroecological market organized by Heifer, where she sells her produce alongside other farmers every Wednesday.

Yumara Salas Ramírez, 30, lives in Santa Rita, a community in the Sierra Madre de Chiapas, among coffee farms and dense forest at the edge of the El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve. A single mother to her daughter Ximena, she works at the Sierra Azul Cooperative’s collection center, where she checks coffee quality and is learning to cup. She was the first woman to serve as the cooperative’s secretary and is part of Café 89, the coffee brand of the cooperative’s women producers, created to make their work visible. Chiapas grows 41% of Mexico’s coffee, yet women hold only about a quarter of Mexico’s ejido land rights. Yumara speaks openly about the machismo that still holds women back, and about a region hit by drug-trafficking violence, climate change, and pests such as the coffee berry borer. Still, she chose to stay.

Yumara Salas Ramírez picks coffee during the harvest on the hillsides of Santa Rita, Chiapas.

Salas Ramírez rakes the coffee at the processing mill to ensure it dries evenly.

Salas Ramírez and Anayanci Domínguez Vazquez smell the cups during a cupping session at the Sierra Azul Cooperative.

Aurelia Beb Tec, 44, grows cacao on five manzanas (about eight and a half acres) in Pinares, a Maya Q’eqchi’ village in Alta Verapaz. Every Wednesday she walks the slopes with her daughters Brenda, Mayra, and Mirna, picking the ripe pods and selling the harvest to the local association. She planted every tree herself. At home she roasts the beans on a clay comal, grinds them on stone, and makes hot chocolate, while her daughters learn to make bars with cardamom and milk.

For decades the Q’eqchi’ of Pinares were dispossessed by landowners and forced into servitude; then came repression and civil war. After the peace accords, a reparations program brought land, seeds, and support, and cacao proved the best crop. In 2014 the community founded APIDIP (Asociación del Pueblo Indígena para el Desarrollo Integral Productivo de la Aldea Pinares), which today has 156 members and exports fair trade, organic cacao.

Aurelia Beb Tec walks among the cacao trees in the rain, searching for ripe pods during the harvest.

Beb Tec and her daughter Brenda sort cacao in their kitchen.

Lucianie Vil, 70, is a Madan Sara, one of the women traders who travel Haiti’s roads and markets to support their families and feed their communities. She lives in Ma Rouge, a scattered village in the mountains of southeastern Haiti. Every Wednesday she walks up to her plot in Thiotte, where she harvests pineapples, oranges, passion fruit, and coffee with her husband and grandchildren, then carries her harvest down the mountain by mule and sells it at the border market of Anse-à-Pitre on Fridays. More than half of Haiti’s population now faces food insecurity, and rural trade depends on routes increasingly cut off by violence and on harvests threatened by drought. Lucianie started selling at 13 and raised seven children on what the land gave her. Like the bird the Madan Sara are named after, she never stops moving.

On a narrow mountain trail, Lucianie Vil walks ahead of a mule loaded with fruit and vegetables on the three- hour journey from Romain to her home in Ma Rouge.

Vil clears a path with her machete through the undergrowth on her plot in Romain.

Vil counts the day’s earnings with a fellow vendor at the market in Anse-à-Pitre. She reports that a day at the market brings in around $150 in sales, of which she keeps roughly $100 once transport and other costs are paid.

Before dawn at Heifer Ranch, Samantha Noble already has her boots on. She checks the mobile chicken coops, looks over the birds, and plans with her team which paddock to move that day. Born in Minnesota in 1993, she grew up around animals and ended up studying animal science.

A professor told her about Heifer International and she came to the ranch as a volunteer, first guiding school visits, then rotating among livestock species. Poultry has been her trade ever since, and today she is the ranch’s poultry production coordinator. Heifer Ranch, about 40 miles west of Little Rock, is a living laboratory for regenerative livestock farming, where planned grazing, holistic management, and animal health are researched and demonstrated. Her goal is to help other producers save time, improve their farms, and find a better balance between work and life.

Morning fog over the ranch roads in Perryville, Arkansas.

Noble, the ranch’s poultry production coordinator, walks through one of the mobile coops built on the pasture.

Noble takes two of her children to a swimming lesson.

Milexy Rodríguez, 46, lives in El Nance, a rural community in Olanchito, in the department of Yoro. Over the years, she built up a cattle farm that supported her family. But in 2023 the lagoon her herd depended on dried up, and in just 40 days she lost 15 cows. To stop relying on rain alone, she drilled a well and began to diversify, and today she raises cattle, grows chili peppers, and keeps a small apiary with her daughter. Honduras is facing a new water emergency, and producers in Yoro report a sharp drop in the milk reaching collection centers. Rural women also face barriers to credit and resources. Milexy belongs to a community savings group and shares what she has learned as a community leader and trainer.

Milexy Rodríguez, in a blue shirt and hat, and her daughter Nayeli, in white, at a cattle fair held one evening around the CREL, the community milk collection center, in a neighboring village. Organized by local ranching families, these gatherings bring neighbors together and offer a break from the daily rhythm of work on the ranch.

Rodríguez milks one of her cows on the ranch. Today she gets fewer than 10 liters a day, far below what she produced before losing her herd in the 2023 drought.

A calf feeds from its mother on Rodríguez’s ranch.

Milexy Rodríguez rides home on her motorcycle after delivering her milk to the El Edén collection center.

The project was produced with support from Heifer International.

#6623. Our 11 Favorite Watches Coming to the Biggest Auctions of the Year

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

This is the biggest weekend of the year for vintage watches. It’s the year-end watch auctions in Geneva, where many prestigious houses bring their very best pieces to market. And it’s never been a more enthralling time to keep a close eye on what happens in Geneva over the next few days. In the first half of the year, the number of million-dollar watches nearly eclipsed the total for the entirety of 2025. A couple of the pieces listed below, including a unique Rolex and a rare Patek Philippe in stainless steel, have estimates above a million bucks.

Writer Oren Hartov and I pored over hundreds of lots to bring you our 11 favorite watches plus one bonus selection. See them all below.

You know a banger is coming up for sale when the house behind it doesn’t even bother capping its price range. Auction estimates are routinely and famously low to encourage bidders, and this watch’s starting point is still $1.2 million. Why? Well, have you ever seen a Rolex like this before? Before Rolex defined the look of modern watches with pieces like the Submariner, it operated similarly to many other manufacturers in Switzerland, willing to make one-off pieces and experiment frequently with its design.

This square beauty from the early 1940s is “most probably unique,” as Phillips auction house writes in its essay on the piece. This exact piece last hit the auction block in 2004, and no other example has come up for public sale since. It’s crazy to see how much this watch’s case shape resembles Heuer’s similarly blocky Monaco, which wouldn’t be released for another 25-plus years. Unfortunately, as cool as this watch is, it does not come with onyx prayer beads. —Cam Wolf

There’s Patek, then there’s complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples in insane condition. This watch checks all those boxes. A reference 1436, it’s a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph, meaning it can time successive intervals of a race or event. One of just two stainless steel examples known to the market, it has an estimate of $2.4-$4.8M, a testament to its rarity and importance. —Oren Hartov

Yet another rare watch executed in stainless steel, this fabulous Lange 1 boasts a gorgeous two-tone dial in blue, with darker subdials contrasting against a cobalt-colored main dial. Dating to 1999 and first sold by the German retailer Oeding-Erdel, it’s one of approximately 30 pieces made in the most utilitarian of metals. Originally fitted with a more standard silvered dial, it received its current navy-blue dial as a replacement and is one of just two stainless steel Lange 1s known in this particular configuration. —OH

Renewed interest in Urban Jürgensen stemming from its recent relaunch under the directorship of Kari Voutilainen, who has since left the CEO position but remains on the company’s board, has seen watches such as this early-’90s ref. 2 garner more attention. A lovely perpetual calendar-moonphase, it’s housed in a classically inspired 37.7mm yellow gold case with cornes-de-vache-style lugs, a stepped bezel, and an incredible dial with the brand’s signature observatory-style hands. Someone tell Timothée Chalamet. —OH

Chopard has a hard-earned reputation for putting out some of the most finely made watches in Switzerland. It’s not just the nerds who are familiar with its work anymore, either. If we (the nerds, obviously) were sending a watch in a bottle to help share that message far and wide, this Lunar One, which looks like something out of Superman’s icy Fortress of Solitude, wouldn’t be a bad choice. This is Chopard’s first watch to combine a perpetual calendar and a moonphase, which is like shaving truffles on caviar. I love that the Roman numerals at 4 and 8 o’clock look like columns nearly buckling under the weight of the center of the dial. This watch also comes with several fun add-ons, like onyx prayer beads plus a ring and a pen set with diamonds. —Cam Wolf

While many younger collectors are obsessed with the Cosmograph Daytona, true “Crown” heads know that other pre-Daytona chronographs sometimes present an even more compelling proposition. This ref. 3525 ‘’Bariletto,’ dating to the 1940s, is not only the first Oyster-cased Rolex chronograph, but it’s also the only known stainless-steel example carrying the signature on the dial of Proud’s, a Rolex retailer based in Sydney. Manually wound, paired to a handsome beads-of-rice bracelet, and measuring a compact 36mm, it comes from the collection of important Italian collector Pucci Papaleo. —OH

While this stainless steel Patek may look like a normal ref. 2509—a beautiful hand-wound dress watch from the midcentury—it’s actually a “school watch” modified by a watchmaking student at the Geneva Watchmaking School. Dating to the 1960s, it’s housed in a 35mm stainless steel case and features a lovely dial with the ‘Ecole d’Horlogerie Geneve’ signature instead of Patek Philippe’s. Open it up, and the hand-wound movement is signed by Norbert Henry, the watchmaking student who assembled and finished it. While it may not attract the attention of more typical Patek collectors, its under-the-radar qualities make it a potential sleeper hit. —OH

It’s tough to argue with the sheer beauty of Vacheron’s mid-20th-century output, much of which is vastly underappreciated compared to comparable pieces from the likes of Patek Philippe. This splendid yellow gold ref. 4072 with a two-tone multi-scale dial dates to the late 1940s—one of my favorite eras of watch design. Powered by the hand-wound cal. V 492 movement and featuring a lovely set of long, contoured lugs, its dial is in fantastic condition, with applied dart and Roman indices, sharp printing, a crisp signature, and legible tachymeter and telemeter scales. It will surely find its way onto the wrist of a collector with excellent taste. —OH

This watch’s dial depicts Saint George, who, according to legend, slew a dragon while on horseback. This is a perfect use for the rich, deep colors you get from enamel. The flames licking at Saint George are beautiful shades of orange and red. He triumphantly lifts his spear as his steed rears its front legs. It’s very cool how much story you can get from this little 35mm timepiece. —CW

Watch collectors might pony up a few thousand for one of independent watchmaker F.P. Journe’s used tissues at this point. However, they’ll have to settle for a host of accessories coming to auction instead this weekend. The maker is so in-demand that, in addition to his timepieces, houses are selling his empty watch boxes and a set of toys that resemble him. This lot is in the middle of those two extremes: a wall clock made to resemble Journe’s Octa Réserve de Marche. Although I’m not gonna lie, flipping this over and seeing the compartment where you stuff in the batteries is a bit of a buzzkill. —CW

They used to make everything look more elegant. This original Longines design was developed in 1931 with famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. It is technically a pilot’s watch, but its elegant, icy-blue dial and Roman numerals would make it the fanciest model on many red carpets in 2026. This is a model from the ‘80s inspired by that original design, and it comes on an absolutely righteous beads-of-rice bracelet. Someone is going to get this guy for around $2,500 if the estimate is correct! —CW

In Rolex world, even the advertisements sell for thousands of dollars. It’s hard to blame people when we’re talking about a rare poster of a GMT-Master wearing a snow-dusted Rolex beanie. Awwww. (Relatedly, imagine if Rolex sold that beanie!? Oh, boy.) —CW

#6622. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6620. All of the Best Looks From the 2026 LACMA Art + Film Gala

Last night, the 2026 LACMA Art + Film Gala took place at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art in California. The night, co-chaired by actor Leonardo DiCaprio and trustee Eva Chow, brought together influential figures from the worlds of art, film, fashion, and entertainment to support the museum’s mission to make film more central to its future programming. Artist Vija Celmins and filmmaker Denis Villeneuve also received special honors.

Before the ceremony began, the red carpet saw a legion of Hollywood A-listers sport their most grand styles. Every year, the LACMA Gala—which is supported by Gucci—produces memorable (and extremely glamorous) formal attire moments, and this evening was sure no different.

Last year saw some of newly-installed creative director Demna’s first big red carpet moments, like stars Elle Fanning and Doja Cat appearing in their boldest looks by the Italian label. This year saw things amp up even more: Kim Kardashian played with her enduring love of the cut-out in a Bordeaux-toned sequin dress, while Parker Posey looked radiant in a sparkling white kaftan. Sienna Miller made the case for the LSD (the Little Silver Dress) while Rose Huntington-Whiteley went to glamorous extremes with some serious skin on show—all were care of Gucci.

And while Gucci was well represented across the evening, striking looks were also served courtesy of Valentino, Saint Laurent, and Chanel. Want to see all of the celebrities who dominated the LACMA Art + Film Gala this year? See Vogue’s roundup of the very best looks here. And be sure to vote on who you think was the very best dressed of the evening.

#6619. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6618. Have Yourself A Chrissy Little Christmas

Chrissy Teigen is trading a picture-perfect holiday for homemade ornaments, flour-dusted counters, and a verrry full house.

Christmas for Chrissy Teigen, cookbook author and founder of the food and bakeware brand Cravings by Chrissy Teigen, means getting the whole crew together: her husband, award-winning artist and producer John Legend; their four kids; three dogs; a bearded dragon; and a parrot. There’s a lot going on under one roof.But Chrissy handles chaos with ease. These days, she’s more focused on making memories with Luna, 10, Miles, 8, Esti, 3, and Wren, 3, than on making everything perfect.Much of that joy happens in the kitchen, where Chrissy has built a career writing three best-selling cookbooks and launching a line of baking mixes in unexpected flavors, like snickerdoodle with miso-honey sugar.The family travels often, but Chrissy is looking forward to staying put this winter. It’ll give her more space to embrace the spontaneity she’s craving this year—the kind you can find only when you’re home for the holidays.

Chrissy Teigen: Oh, Halloween. We have a big kids’ Halloween party here at the house. We pick a theme and run with it. This year we picked Coraline.

We love crafting so much. I wanted to stay home for the holidays this year because I need all my children to start hand-making their ornaments and putting them on the tree. I’ve entered this time in my life where I want Christmas to be completely whimsical and over the top. I want to have a cute, colorful, chaotic Christmas this year. I want to thread the popcorn onto the string and have the most chaotic kids’ Christmas tree ever. And I can’t wait for that.

Cooking, of course. Scalloped potatoes in my house are very, very holiday. And my mom comes to town. She lives in Thailand, so we love getting the whole family together. And there’s a lot of football. John’s family loves it, and there’s usually a big Ohio State game around Thanksgiving that they all go crazy for. They go just as nuts for the Christmas game, too. It’s very much the whole family on the floor of my house, watching everything together, and it’s beautiful.

It will be filled with so much joy, but it’s going to be an emotional one for me, of course. To have that big yellow chair that my dad loved so much, empty...I don’t exactly know what to expect from me emotionally, but I can imagine it will be all the things that make the holidays so complex: sad and wonderful and special all at the same time.We will bake, with love, the potatoes Dad loved so, so much. We will clean the greens the way Granny (on John’s side) told us to. I’m sure our eyes will well up. It’ll be a testament to how much they meant to us all.

It is, but that recipe has always haunted me. My mom is impossible to get a recipe from. I think a lot of moms do this on purpose: You ask them to share a recipe, and something’s missing, or they leave out one little thing.I’ve checked in about this one so many times. She’s made it twice a year my whole life, and every time I ask about a detail—whether she uses MSG or when she adds the pepper—I get a different answer. So I’m not even sure I have the right recipe in my cookbook. Whenever she makes it, something is different. You could call it a mom’s touch, but I think she’s leaving out an important ingredient because she wants hers to be the best.

We do Tyler Florence’s beef Wellington every year. It looks impressive, but it’s quite simple, and it’s never gone wrong for me. When I cut into it, the color is beautiful, and it’s juicy. Over the years, I’ve learned how to keep the pastry crisp, even on the bottom where the meat juices collect. It’s a flawless recipe, and the peppercorn sauce is amazing. It pleases everyone, and the kids can cut shapes out of the puff pastry. For sides, we have the scalloped potatoes, green beans, and carrots.

My girls are always in the kitchen with me—I’m not allowed to cook without them. I love it, even though it slows things down. Esti is kind of the boss of the house right now, and she gets nervous that if she goes upstairs to shower, we’ll finish the recipe without her. We make sure she’s back in time to cook the recipe from beginning to end. I expect Esti and Luna will do most of the cooking for Christmas dinner.

No, they’re more likely to spill things. The living room is always covered in spills. I often put my drink on the floor because the table is too far away, and the boys knock it over with their feet.

Miles is our “won’t eat anything” guy. He’s eight now, and he’s been picky since he started eating solid food. He mostly likes chicken nuggets, fries, hamburgers, and pizza. Esti’s tastes change quickly. She might want apples with every dinner, then decide she doesn’t like them—and be like, “I never liked apples. Are you crazy?”Wren is our tank. He’ll eat anything. He gets almost catatonic when he’s eating, so he forgets it could make him sick.Luna knows how to make foods taste better. If something has a burnt corner, for example, she’ll cut it off or find another way to improve it. I think that’s really special.

I remember not liking raw tomatoes or avocados when I was young, even though I love them now, so I’m not too worried about how the kids’ tastes will change. They’re kids, and they’re told what to do all day. Food can be one way they speak up and feel like their opinions matter. I get that—it must be hard to be told what to do from morning to night. As long as they’re full and not waking up hungry, I’m fine.

Christmas morning is an all-day experience for us. Once my kids open a present, they want to play with it, so they take their time instead of rushing through the gifts. I used to have so many rules and run around stressing about the wrapping and recycling. Now I just relax and let the day unfold.

I love prepping for Christmas the night before, especially when it’s a secret, and I’m in charge. I’ll make hot cocoa bombs. In the morning, the kids just have to pour hot milk over them. And we’ll have pancakes, bacon, and Mrs. Butterworth’s syrup, get a sugar rush, and then hopefully have like a nice midday crash together.

Luna has always wanted to be in on the secret. I worried that, as my oldest, she might feel like she was missing out on the Christmas magic, but she loves helping make it special for her younger siblings. Last year, I asked if she wanted to stay up all night with me, and she loved that more than anything.She and Esti also love making stockings for the dogs, the bearded dragon, and now the parrot. We had lots of animals growing up, and I remember my mom taking me to PetSmart to pick out little gifts for our bird. I made sure every beating heart in the house got celebrated, and now the kids love doing that, too.

The bearded dragon toy industry is small. Last year we got little inflatable pools, and there are dried insects, as gross as they are. And a little Santa hat. He’s happy with that. I used to make bird toys with my dad for our parrot, so getting things for Audrey reminds me of that time with him.

Without a doubt, and I’m putting Luna in charge. Carrot cake is our family’s favorite. It was my wedding cake, and it’s John’s family’s favorite, too. There’s so much warmth in it: It has spices and real carrots, and it’s sticky, decadent, and delicious. It’s our holiday pleaser.In addition to our carrot cake kit, I hope we can one day offer a kit with lots of elements for people to decorate a cake and have fun with. The holidays are all about slowing down and getting your hands into something, and it doesn’t hurt if you can eat it after, too.

No, but I loved baking mixes, especially confetti cake mix. My dad had a big sweet tooth, and baking mixes and TV dinners were important to me. My mom’s food seemed too spicy or daunting when I was a kid, so my dad and I bonded over Hungry-Man dinners, Kid Cuisine, and Hot Pockets. Homemade food was mostly for the holidays.I think that’s why grocery stores still excite me. I take my kids shopping and love seeing what’s new—and finding foods that taste just like I remember, like frozen Salisbury steak. Those were the foods I grew up on, and I wanted to recreate them at home for my Cravings cookbooks. I’ve never looked down on those foods. They’ve stood the test of time for a reason. They’re nostalgic and wonderful.

#6617. Kylie Jenner Has Called It: It’s Fawn Girl Fall

Kylie Jenner is no deer in the headlights, but she decided to go full fawn at the LACMA Art+Film Gala on Saturday night. Making her debut at the annual Los Angeles event to fundraise for the museum, the beauty mogul joined a starry crowd embracing all things glitzy and gloriously extravagant. For many, that meant a lot of sequins and skin-baring. But for Jenner, that meant a shimmering, body-skimming gown in fashion’s latest animal-print obsession: deer spots.

The dress, from Ashi Studio’s fall 2026 couture collection, was an on-trend departure from the usual leopard and zebra. Cut close to the body in a mottled chocolate-brown and silver fabric that resembled the delicate markings of a fawn, it featured a high halter neckline, a sculpted waist, and a floor-grazing skirt that flared gently from the knees. The original runway design featured tiny, sculptural antlers protruding from the collar, though these appear to have been removed for Jenner’s red-carpet outing.

It was also all business in the front, tassel in the back: the otherwise streamlined gown opened to reveal almost her entire back, with a swirling and shimmering tassel tracing down her spine. It was a little nod to the opulent, old-world glamour currently making its way back into fashion, which has been dominated by luxe detailing: swishing fringe, ornamental frog clasps, oversized bows, and fur-trimmed robes abound right now. More is more, particularly when it comes to the finer details.

Styled by Rose Grandquist and Mackenzie Grandquist, Jenner kept the rest of the look signature sultry. Hairstylist Igor Rosales-Jackson fashioned her jet-black lengths into a glossy, center-parted cascade of voluptuous waves, while makeup artist Ariel Tejada opted for fluttery lashes, softly bronzed cheeks, and a nude-pink lip. Zola Ganzorigt was behind her understated manicure, with jewelry by Lorraine Schwartz adding a final glint.

Jenner is hardly the first to go wild for the print. After years of leopard and zebra reigning supreme, fashion’s animal kingdom has welcomed a gentler, more woodland-inspired contender. Katie Holmes was an early adopter, stepping out in deer-spotted Tory Burch, while Sofia Richie Grainge gave the pattern her quiet-luxury seal of approval with a jacket and sleeveless maxi dress in the debut collection of her label, SRG. On the runways, the interpretations have been considerably more daring. For spring 2027, LaQuan Smith made Bambi print decidedly grown-up, working it into barely-there minidresses, sculpted jackets, and slinky combinations with flashes of lilac lingerie. Baum und Pferdgarten got in on the action by incorporating the motif into its playful, ballet-inspired collection. Elsewhere, British label Cawley Studio has taken a more heritage-minded approach, offering deer-spotted leather flying jackets and pillbox hats, while Carelli has brought the pattern into the realm of plush, statement-making outerwear.

There’s a surprising amount of versatility to the Bambi print. Where leopard has long carried a certain strain of bombshell bravado (remember the “mob wife” trend of yore?), deer spots feel softer and more romantic. Rendered in caramel and cream shades, it works particularly well with fall’s appetite for textures, suede, shearling, and rich, earthy tones. But, as Kylie Jenner proved, the print can look just as at home under the flashbulbs as it does on a countryside ramble

That was certainly the spirit of the evening. The 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala red carpet was a veritable parade of shine, sparkle, and high-octane glamour, from Kim Kardashian’s oxblood Gucci sequins to the dramatic cutouts of Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. Jenner’s metallic deer look fit right in. This fall, fashion has a new creature to fawn over.

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

#6614. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.
