#6556. Dry-Brined Turkey With Tangy Honey Glaze

This dry-brine turkey recipe produces a Thanksgiving centerpiece that’s full of flavor and juicy as heck. The brine is just kosher salt and brown sugar, applied at least 12 hours and up to 2 days ahead. The salt helps the meat retain moisture, while an uncovered rest in the fridge dries the skin for better browning—no bucket required.

Roasting the bird on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet (instead of a high-sided roasting pan) lets hot air circulate around it, encouraging browning all over. We’ve also done away with the turkey baster in favor of a buttery honey-vinegar glaze you’ll brush over the bird while it cooks. Fragrant with rosemary, garlic, and orange zest, with Worcestershire sauce for savory depth, the repeated brushing builds an even, glossy lacquer.

Let the cooked turkey rest uncovered for 30 minutes to 1 hour before carving. Resist the urge to tent it with foil, which traps steam and softens that hard-earned crispy skin. Use the downtime to put the finishing touches on your Thanksgiving side dishes.

What kind of turkey should I buy for dry-brining?

Choose an unseasoned turkey. Kosher, self-basting, and enhanced turkeys have already been salted, so adding this dry brine can make them overly salty. Check the label for an added salt solution before buying. A frozen turkey is fine; thaw it in the refrigerator for at least 24 hours before starting the brine.

No. In this recipe, the brine stays on the bird; Step 2 calls for rinsing the baking sheet and rack to prevent the drippings from becoming too salty, not the turkey. Follow the measurement for your brand of kosher salt, and don’t feel compelled to use every last grain of the mixture—the recipe intentionally makes extra.

Yes, but taste them first: The dry brine and glaze make these drippings especially flavorful, and they may be quite salty. Skim off the excess fat to make your roux, then add the juices a little at a time, followed by low-sodium chicken broth (or homemade unseasoned turkey stock).

Our Make-Ahead Gravy doesn’t need drippings, but you can stir some in as it reheats. Taste before adding salt.

Can I use a larger or spatchcocked turkey?

Yes, but not with the same roasting schedule. This dry brine recipe is written for a whole 12–14-lb. bird; a larger turkey or one that’s been flattened will cook differently. For a spatchcocked bird, follow our Spatchcock Turkey With Anise and Orange rather than transferring this recipe’s roasting and glazing times.

See why each step works in our guide to cooking Thanksgiving turkey →

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 12 hours brining

Place ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar in a small bowl and work together with your fingers until incorporated. Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck reserved for gravy, giblets discarded, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and pat dry with paper towels. (If you don’t have this setup, place your turkey on a V-shape rack set inside a large roasting pan.) Sprinkle salt mixture all over outside of the turkey as well as inside the cavity of the turkey, patting to adhere and nudging some into every crevice. You won’t need all of the dry brine, but it’s good to have extra since some of it will end up on the baking sheet as you season the turkey. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid onto pan). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil and set rack back inside. Place turkey, breast side up, on rack and tuck wings underneath. Let turkey sit at room temperature 2–3 hours.

Place an oven rack in middle of oven; preheat oven to 450°. Using your fingers, loosen turkey skin on breast. Work 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, under skin, spreading evenly over both breasts. Smear outside of turkey with another 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature.

Tie legs together with kitchen twine and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet.

Roast turkey, rotating pan halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown all over, about 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook ¼ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. honey, 4 tsp. Worcestershire sauce, 3 sprigs rosemary, 3 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, and remaining 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, in a small saucepan over medium heat until bubbling and slightly thickened, about 5 minutes. Reduce heat to lowest setting and keep glaze warm.

Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 30 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast near the neck registers 155° (don’t worry; the temperature will continue to climb while the bird rests), 65–85 minutes longer. Skin should be deep golden brown, shiny, and crisp. Transfer turkey to a cutting board and let rest at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour before carving.

#6555. This Coffee Subscription Delivers Some of the Freshest Beans We’ve Tried

It's one of the best gifts you can give to coffee lovers this holiday season.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

It really doesn't get fresher than this. A Storyville coffee subscription delivers delicious beans right to your doorstep.

We’ve all been there. Standing in the grocery store staring at dozens of coffee brands and trying to decide which one might perk us up, only to end up scowling at a subpar cup of sludge the next morning. Well, those days are over because Storyville, one of Seattle’s best coffee shops, now delivers freshly roasted beans straight to your door.

I tried a Storyville coffee subscription, and I assure you that you’ll never have to waste your time (or money) on stale beans again. Here’s everything you need to know about this caffeinated club.

Storyville is one of the highest-rated coffee shops in Seattle, with locations at Pike Place and at 1st and Madison. They also have a roasting studio you can tour to see exactly where your coffee beans are roasted before making their way to your door. But if you can’t make it to Seattle, they also offer coffee subscription services with nationwide shipping.

The brand sources premium-grade green coffees and roasts each bean varietal individually before blending. Beans are roasted on the darker end of medium and feature a rich, natural sweetness with notes of chocolate and caramel. Unlike many other dark roasts, this coffee has a smooth finish and no bitterness. Best of all, Storyville ships its coffee immediately after roasting.

Storyville subscriptions are highly customizable in order to fit your needs. First, choose between whole beans and single-serve pods. Then choose the quantity and delivery frequency that best suits your needs. You can pause, skip or cancel via text at any time. Moreover, you’ll receive 20% off, among other perks.

I am a coffee fiend. On any given day, I’m three cups in by 9 a.m. That’s why I couldn’t wait to get my hands on a bag of real Seattle coffee.

My order arrived on Wednesday, October 28. I received a bag of Prologue coffee beans, Sunrise espresso beans and Epilogue decaf coffee beans. I knew the roast dates would be stamped on the bags, but I was amazed to see that my beans had been roasted just days prior, on October 25 and October 27. Talk about fresh!

I opened the Prologue first and poured the entire bag into the bean hopper of my De’Longhi Rivelia. After brewing, I took a sip before adding my cream and sugar and was amazed by how smooth it was. It was fresh and flavorful without a hint of bitterness. I love a dark roast and could drink this all day long.

The next day, I opened the Sunrise espresso beans. I used it to make a regular cup of coffee followed by an Americano. Like the Prologue, the beans were clearly fresh, and the coffee was exceptionally smooth! I’ll be saving this bag along with the decaf for espresso martinis with my girlfriends.

As a dark roast gal, I’ve had my fair share of coffee that tastes bitter or burnt. I didn’t get any notes of bitterness from Storyville coffee. I’ll also point out that a bag of Prologue coffee lasted one week. Given how much coffee I drink plus the fact that my husband tends to make a cup here and there, I’m not surprised we went through it so quickly. Luckily, the subscription is completely customizable. If you drink as much coffee as I do, you’ll want to order two or three bags at a time. But if you just enjoy one cup per day, then one bag at a time will suffice.

That said, these beans are so fresh we wouldn’t be surprised if you start drinking more coffee than usual. And we certainly wouldn’t blame you!

It’s also easy to send a subscription as a gift. Simply head over to their gifting page and opt for three, five, eight or 12 prepaid shipments.

#6554. Cranberry Brie Wontons

If your friends love our cranberry brie bites, they’ll go nuts for these cranberry brie wontons. Brushed with butter and air-fried until crispy on the outside and gooey in the middle, these wontons are the party snack you need this holiday season. Don’t forget the bowl of cranberry sauce for dunking—it makes it feel extra-festive.

Stuffing the wontons:In order to have a satisfactorily cheesy center after the wontons are fried, you’ll need to cram a lot of brie into the wonton when stuffing it. Brie shrinks a lot when it melts, so while a 1/2-ounce cube might feel like a lot, it’s actually the perfect amount.

Cooking the wontons:While wontons are often deep-fried, I opted for the air fryer here since it makes for faster, easier cleanup and still yields a delicious result. Yes, the wontons don’t get quite as bubble-textured or evenly browned as they would if they were deep-fried, but they still crisp up really nicely—and the butter adds a delightful flavor all on its own!

Make-ahead tips:Once cooked, these wontons are best eaten immediately. But if you want to make ahead, you can form and freeze the wontons for up to 1 month. Freeze on a parchment-lined baking sheet until hard, then transfer to an airtight container. Wontons that have been totally frozen might take a few extra minutes to air-fry!

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

María de los Ángeles Orfila is a science journalist from Montevideo, Uruguay, known for her long-form writing featured in El País and El Observador. She also participated in the Sharon Dunwoody Mentoring Program 2023 offered by The Open Notebook and has bylines in Science, Scientific American, and Discover Magazine, among other outlets.

#6552. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6551. This Old-School Drink Is Making a Comeback for the Coziest Winter Cocktails

Port isn't just for sipping after dinner. We asked a respected winemaker about how this rich, fruity wine can be used to make easy winter cocktails.

For my birthday, a friend gifted me a bottle of Angel’s Envy bourbon. It was a fantastic gift (thank you, Jaclyn!), but what stood out to me was a detail on the label: “finished in port wine barrels.”

Usually I hear of bourbon barrels being used to age other things. The Goose Island Bourbon County Stout, for example, is a beer that’s aged in bourbon barrels, and it’s so special that people will line up outside grocery stores in the hope of grabbing a pack. But I’m less familiar with port wine, and I wanted to learn more.

I’ve been seeing port pop up on menus and in cocktail recipes with more frequency. When I think of port, I imagine the nobility in medieval times sipping from big pewter goblets. Of course, you don’t need to be a royal to enjoy it!

I reached out to an expert for some advice on how to incorporate port into more of my winter cocktails. He gave me a crash course in everything I needed to know about the wine, and shared some of the best ways to use it in cocktails.

I connected with David Guimaraens, head winemaker for Taylor Fladgate. Born in Portugal, David is the sixth generation of his family to be involved in the port business. He’s widely recognized as one of the most gifted winemakers in the modern port industry, and his tips on how to winterize cocktails with port are simple enough to incorporate into any cocktail routine.

Taste of Home: For someone who may be unfamiliar with the category, how would you explain what port is and what distinguishes it from other styles of wine?

David Guimaraens: Port is a fortified wine produced in Portugal’s Douro Valley, one of the world’s oldest demarcated wine regions. What sets it apart is that a small amount of grape spirit is added during fermentation. This stops the fermentation process so some of the natural sweetness from the grapes remains in the finished product. The result is a uniquely rich, concentrated fruit wine with an incredible depth of flavor.

There are many different styles of port, from fresh, vibrant ruby ports to complex, aged tawnies and exceptional vintage ports. That diversity makes port a far more versatile category than many people realize, with styles suited to everything from cocktails and aperitifs to food pairings and after-dinner enjoyment.

TOH: What qualities does port bring to a mixed drink, and why does it work particularly well as a cocktail ingredient?

DG: Port brings fruit notes, sweetness and complexity to a cocktail. Depending on the style, its flavor profile can range from fresh berry and spice to dried fruit, nuts and caramel. It is remarkably versatile behind the bar. Port can replace or complement vermouth and other sweet components in classic cocktails. Its concentration of flavor allows you to add complexity to a drink without a long list of ingredients.

TOH: Why is port trending for winter cocktails and seasonal entertaining?

DG: There is something naturally comforting about port during the colder months. Its fruit and spice notes pair particularly well with seasonal flavors such as cranberry, orange, cinnamon, ginger and chocolate, making it a versatile choice for holiday entertaining. Port has also always been a wine for sharing. Serving it in a cocktail or a simple spritz offers a more informal, contemporary way to enjoy that tradition and bring port to the table.

TOH: For someone experimenting with port cocktails at home for the first time, what is the easiest way to begin? Are there simple serves, ratios or ingredient pairings you recommend?

DG: Keep it simple. You don’t need to be a mixologist to make a great port cocktail. A port spritz is an easy place to start: Serve port over plenty of ice, top with sparkling water or tonic, and finish with a slice or twist of fresh citrus. It is refreshing, simple to prepare and easy to adapt to your own taste.

TOH: For consumers shopping for port to use in cocktails, what should they look for when selecting a bottle? Does someone need to invest in an expensive Port to make a great cocktail?

DG: Absolutely not. In fact, I would reserve great vintage ports for enjoying on their own!

For cocktails, look for a good-quality, fruit-driven reserve ruby port with enough character to stand up alongside the other ingredients. Fonseca Bin 27 is a great example: It is approachable and full of rich berry fruit, and it has the structure and depth to work extremely well in cocktails.

Have you made port cocktails before? Let us know your favorite version in the comments below!

#6550. Chrissy Teigen Reveals What Her Four Kids Actually Eat

Even cookbook authors can't escape chicken nuggets.

You’d think having Chrissy Teigen as your mom would mean enjoying some pretty incredible meals every day. After all, she’s a cookbook author with her own food brand, Cravings, and is constantly experimenting with new recipes. But apparently, even Teigen can’t get all four of her kids to agree on dinner.

During a recent episode of Déjà Food, Teigen opened up about mealtime with her husband, John Legend, and their four children, Luna, Miles, Esti, and Wren.

“We are in this stage right now where nobody really wants to eat the same meal, but we also aren’t a restaurant,” Teigen explains when asked about the last meal all four children ate together.

“I can almost guarantee your answer is chicken nuggets and Kraft macaroni and cheese,” she says. “And then I get whatever is left on the baking sheet.”

And in an exclusive interview with Delish, Teigen reveals just how different her children's eating habits really are.

Miles, 8, is apparently the pickiest of the bunch. “Miles is our ‘won't eat anything’ guy,” she admits, explaining that he’s been selective about food since he started eating solids. His preferred foods include chicken nuggets, fries, hamburgers, and pizza.

Esti, 3, is a little less predictable. According to Teigen, she might insist on having apples with every dinner one day, only to decide she doesn’t like them the next.

Wren, meanwhile, is the complete opposite of his older brother. “Wren is our tank. He’ll eat anything,” Teigen says.

And then there’s Luna, 10, who appears to have inherited her mom’s interest in cooking. Teigen explains that Luna knows how to improve dishes, whether that means cutting off a burnt corner or finding another way to make something taste better.

In fact, Luna and Esti are regulars in the kitchen. Teigen says her daughters are so involved in cooking that Esti worries she’ll miss part of a recipe if she leaves the room.

But the kids aren’t getting away with chicken nuggets and mac and cheese every single day.

On Déjà Food, Teigen reveals that when developing a Cravings Banana Foster Pancake Mix, her entire family became her unofficial testing panel.

“Every morning, everyone in the whole family has to try our new pancake,” she says, joking that they’re being forced to eat the recipe throughout the week.

Despite everyone’s strong opinions, Teigen isn’t particularly concerned about her children’s changing tastes. She recalls disliking raw tomatoes and avocados when she was younger, even though she loves them now.

“They're kids, and they’re told what to do all day,” she says. “Food can be one way they speak up and feel like their opinions matter.”

It’s a pretty refreshing perspective from someone who’s built a career around food. And considering Teigen grew up loving Hungry-Man dinners, Kid Cuisine, and Hot Pockets herself, perhaps her kids’ appreciation for convenient comfort food shouldn’t be all that surprising.

As long as everyone is fed and happy, she’s not interested in turning dinner into a battle.

#6549. $22 Fries at Marcel Are One of New York's Finest Little Luxuries

This is Highly Recommend, a column dedicated to what we’re eating, drinking, and buying.

I recently celebrated a dear friend's birthday at Marcel 945 Madison, the much buzzed about restaurant at Sotheby's global headquarters (RIP, old Whitney) on the Upper East Side of New York. Inside the Breuer Building, named for its Brutalist architect, it is a space to behold, equal parts concrete and midcentury walnut accents. Every detail—the luscious lighting, the forged flatware, the tufted mohair banquettes—is exquisitely considered and, likely, for sale.

In this beautiful room full of beautiful people, I could not take my eyes off the frites, priced at $22 under the "Accompagnements" section of the menu in Chroma sans serif type.

Skinny but not shoestring, long, golden, and perfectly salted, they practically glowed from within a napkin-lined bread basket. Every frite was pert, not a single one enervated under a mountain of hot fries. There was no oily outline at the bottom, either.

When I first saw the large portion, I felt a brief wave of doubt: Could we even finish these? How silly of me. We made quick work of the basket, with not a single spud left behind. These fries are so good, they do not need the crutch of a condiment—though they did reach another stratosphere when dipped in plain mayonnaise.

“I like them best with the chicken jus in the roasted chicken dish, or sauce au poivre with the filet de boeuf,” recommends Marie-Aude Rose, chef-partner at Marcel.

When people talk about life's little luxuries, they're talking about these frites. If the best McDonald's fries spent a transformative semester in Paris, they would be a little closer—but still untouchable—to Marcel's frites.

Is $22 pricy? Yes. But we're not talking about a paltry handful landing in a stainless steel cup lined with parchment. These are impeccable, best-in-class wonders, elegantly and generously presented.

I was so in awe that I had to know the deliberate thinking that must be responsible for such perfection. Rose says it is a long process. The kitchen begins with Idaho Russet, chosen not just for taste, but for length and sugar and moisture content that she calls “adequate to frying.”

The potatoes are cut with a French fry cutter, soaked in water, then dried and pre-fried in peanut oil at 160C (320F). During service, they are fried again in clean peanut oil at 180C (356F) and then seasoned with La Baleine fine sea salt, Rose’s salt of choice for seasoning all food at the restaurant.

"Time is important,” Rose said. “You cannot rush cooking.”

Please, chef, take all the time you need.

#6548. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6547. Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies Treats

Recipe by Cori Cooper, flagstaff, Arizona

Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats are party-ready, from the bright rainbow colors and fruity flavor to the crisp, chewy texture and marshmallow pull.

If there are Rice Krispies treats on any table full of treats, I’ll make a beeline for them before even glancing at brownies or cupcakes. The combination of light, crisp cereal and chewy marshmallow hits every time. There will always be a place in my heart for the classic ones, but playing around with different Rice Krispies treats variations brings me endless joy. Cori Cooper, a Community Cook from Flagstaff, Arizona, feels the same way, which led her to create these colorful Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats.

By just switching to a rainbow-colored, fruity cereal, Cori transformed the dessert without changing the beloved texture of the original or making it too sweet. I’ll be making these for my next bake sale. Hopefully they make it out of my kitchen!

Place the cereal and half of one package of mini marshmallows in a large bowl.

In a microwave-safe bowl or a large saucepan over low heat, melt the remaining marshmallows in butter, stirring until they’re smooth. Stir in the salt, if using it, then remove the mixture from the heat. Pour it over the cereal mixture.

Editor’s Tip: If using the microwave, heat the butter and marshmallows in 30- to 45-second intervals, stirring in between, to prevent the butter from getting too hot and splattering.

Press into a lightly greased 8-inch square baking pan using waxed paper or a lightly greased spatula. Let the mixture cool to room temperature. Cut it into bars.

Editor’s Tip: For bars that hold together but still have an airy bite and chewy texture, press the cereal mixture evenly into the pan, but don’t use all your might and pack them in.

Store Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats at room temperature, tightly wrapped, for three to five days. Technically, they last longer, but the cereal will start to get stale and the treats will become brittle over time. You can leave the treats in the baking pan and tightly wrap the entire pan, or transfer cut squares to an airtight food storage container, adding a piece of parchment between layers to keep them from sticking together.

You can freeze Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats for up to six weeks, but they won’t have the same soft, stretchy texture as freshly made treats. Pack the treats in a freezer-proof food storage bag, pressing out the excess air, or place them in a container with an airtight lid, adding a piece of parchment between the layers. They will thaw quickly, so just let them stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes before eating them.

Cereal treats can end up hard instead of soft, stretchy and chewy if the marshmallows are stale or overheated, or if you pack the treats too tightly into the baking dish. Stale marshmallows don’t have the same moisture and bounce as fresh ones, making them tough from the start. And since marshmallows are mostly sugar, they can burn or become candy-like if overcooked, which makes the treats unpleasantly firm. If you compress the cereal too much, you crush out all its air, which results in dense treats that are hard to bite through.

You can use several different pans for these Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats to vary their shape or thickness. For thinner treats, press the cereal mixture into a 9-inch square baking pan. For a different shape, use an 8-inch or 9-inch round cake pan and then cut the cereal treats into triangles, like slices of pie.

Since these are Fruity Pebbles treats, you should keep at least half the amount of Fruity Pebbles, but if you’re a few cups short (this happens to me all the time), you can make up the difference with one of the best childhood cereals, like Cheerios or Lucky Charms. You can use almost any crisp, puffed or flaked cereal, but consider what will taste the best with the fruity base. I’d recommend a cereal with light sweetness and a nutty or vanilla flavor so you don’t overshadow the Fruity Pebbles.

#6546. 14 Appetizers That You Can (& Should!) Eat For Dinner

An apps-olutely delicious way to do dinner.

If you’re like me, sometimes you don’t want to make a whole big meal for dinner. A homemade dinner can feel daunting, but I’ll never turn down the opportunity to indulge in appetizers. While it may be frowned upon (though I’d argue wrongfully so) to fill up on pigs in a blanket, stuffed mushrooms, or other finger-food favorites, there are a ton of fantastic appetizers that verge on dinner. It’s those beauties that I turn to for my favorite kinds of evenings: appetizers for dinner! With that in mind, I gathered 14 of our best apps that can (and should) be eaten for dinner. Plus, if you make a few of these on the same night, you’ve got a veritable feast.

Aside from the buttery biscuits, melty provolone cheese, and salty roast beef combo, we’re obsessed with these French dip stuffed biscuits because of how easy (emphasis on easy) they are to make.

These sliders are inspired by a classic fried chicken Caesar salad. They have all the nostalgic flavor notes you love, from crispy fried chicken to a tangy buttermilk dressing.

We love chicken wings in all shapes, sizes, and flavors, but there’s something extra special about the saucy, sweet, savory, and slightly sticky teriyaki wing. Our version skips the store-bought sauce in favor of a few pantry staples that come together in just a few minutes to create a gingery, garlicky soy-based sauce that clings to oven-baked wings and never falls short on flavor.

These old-school sausage pinwheels are a classic for a reason. They feature crescent dough with bits of sausage and red pepper layered within a creamy garlic cheese spread. Bell pepper + cream cheese + cheddar cheese make for a pimento-inspired bite.

What’s better than a tray of cheesy chicken nachos? Four cheese chicken nachos! Don’t worry, though, a couple cans of chopped green chiles cut the richness of all that cheese. We’ll leave the toppings up to you, but we suggest The Works, aka red onion, radishes, avocado, jalapeño, cilantro, and hot sauce.

This recipe has everything you could ever want in the seafood classic: They're golden, crispy, and chock-full of crab flavor. Ready in 30 minutes and served with homemade tartar sauce, they are the perfect easy main or low-effort appetizer.

Sheet-pan quesadillas are easy to assemble and fun to customize to your mood. We were inspired here by our French onion pot roast. In both recipes, we’re utilizing French onion soup packets to get that iconic flavor—no caramelizing onions required.

If you aren’t familiar with the muffuletta sandwich, you should be. It’s filled with three different cured meats, a plethora of olives, roasted red peppers, and other brined ingredients. It’s big and proud, and this dip is the perfect scoopable version of it.

If the best wing flavor and sauce combination is hot Buffalo wings and ranch dip, then it stands to reason that a ranch wing with hot Buffalo dip would be equally delicious—right? Damn right. We flipped the classic combo to create a ranch-flavored chicken wing served with a side of zesty, spicy Buffalo sauce.

This Nashville hot chicken dip brings the heat and MORE. Beware—this party dip is for major spice fans only. A cream cheese, mayo, and sour cream base meets hot sauce and breaded chicken for a spicy, creamy dip that is also perfectly filling.

These sliders are the crème de la crème. Ham, Swiss, and jammy caramelized onions are layered between the star of the show: buttery and soft Hawaiian rolls. You simply split the rolls, layer them, bake, and in a little over 10 minutes, you'll have a dozen hot, mind-blowing sandwiches ready to serve.

Caul us crazy, but we believe that these cauliflower wings are just as good as regular wings. This recipe transforms this staple veggie into crispy, golden bites that were made to be drenched in your favorite sauce.

These vegan potstickers are easy to put together and most of your time is spent roasting your squash until really tender, which can be done ahead of time. Crimping takes a little practice, but the good news is that even if they look a little wonky they are still going to taste great!

In these Buffalo chicken meatballs, ground chicken is formed into meatballs with bread crumbs and plenty of seasoning, before being drenched in the signature hot Buffalo sauce. Ready in 30 minutes, these meatballs are a flavor-packed app you can have ready in no time.

This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6544. Peppermint Bark Cookie Bars

Line a 13×9-inch pan with parchment paper, letting the ends extend up the sides. In a large bowl, use a hand mixer or stand mixer to cream the butter, sugar and vanilla extract until it’s light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Beat in the egg yolks until they’re combined.

In another bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour and salt. Gradually beat the flour mixture into the creamed mixture just until no streaks of flour remain.

In the top of a double boiler or a metal bowl over hot water, melt the dark chocolate, stirring until it’s completely smooth. Remove the bowl from the heat and spread the dark chocolate over the cooled bars.

Editor’s Tip: Never let the water touch the bottom of the bowl, or it will burn the chocolate. Also, try not to get any water into the chocolate, or it will seize.

Repeat the melting and spreading process with the white chocolate, then immediately sprinkle the top with crushed peppermint candies while the chocolate is still wet.

#6543. Think You Don’t Like Broccoli Rabe? You’re Cooking It Wrong

BA’s Best is our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. Today, food director Chris Morocco breaks down his latest recipe, a restaurant-worthy pasta dish you can pull off on a weeknight.

I didn’t grow up with southern Italian dishes like orecchiette with sausage and broccoli rabe, most likely because it originates in Puglia, a region close to my grandmother’s Campania. Her mistrust of the Pugliese, the home province of many of her neighbors in Worcester, MA, was infamous in our family. “Horse eaters” she would whisper, and flick her curtains closed.

Yet this is one of the easiest foundational Italian dishes to make, in a matter of minutes with some basic ingredients. It is balanced in a way that few other pastas could hope for, containing an abundance of greens to counter punchy sausage and handfuls of Parmesan.

Shockingly, Bon Appétit didn’t have a classic recipe for it. That is, until now. I got to work in the Test Kitchen—here are my big takeaways.

Too much ink has been spilled trying to convince home cooks that there are definitive pairings between sauces and pasta shapes. I don’t think your amatriciana gives a hoot if you use strozzapreti or gemelli. Yet I can’t deny the charms of orecchiette for this dish, as the “little ears” are perfectly sized and shaped to cradle nubbins of sausage, and be swaddled by clingy leaves of broccoli rabe. Any short shape will play nicely with the other elements—mezzi rigatoni and lumache especially. Be sure to leave the pasta very al dente before draining, since it will continue cooking with the greens and sausage.

Blanching—a brief dip into simmering salted water—isn’t nearly assertive enough to tame the fibrous stalks of broccoli rabe. To get them truly silky and tender, I give the bottom half of the stalks a 5-minute head start in boiling water, followed by 5-ish more minutes with the tops. There’s no need to shock in ice water or cold water afterward. These fully cooked greens are so luscious, they function almost like a sauce, with some help from cooking liquid and butter.

Italian-style sausage has the sharp scent of fennel, lots of garlic and black pepper, and, in hot varieties, red pepper flakes. If you can find it loose, great, but generally, you will have to remove the casings yourself to reveal the coarsely ground meat. This coarse grind is another key aspect to the dish, as it results in pebble-size chunks that render and crisp without turning into paste.

For years I undercooked my broccoli rabe, barely blanching it to temper some bitterness, yet leaving it so fibrous that even a longer cook with the sausage could never fully unlock its silky potential. I know better now. My colleagues in the Test Kitchen were floored by how delicious an overcooked vegetable can be—how the rabe became creamy like a green sauce, tangling around every other ingredient. It’s not every day you find a dish that you can make just as well as what you might order in a restaurant, after a long work day no less. But this is one of them.

#6542. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.
